extracted.intended_audience: patent litigators and practitioners drafting answers and defenses in equity and patent infringement suits
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and legal standards for formulating answers, special defenses, admissions, and sworn replies in equity suits involving patents, including what must be pleaded with particularity and what evidence is admissible if omitted. Focused on procedural sufficiency and tactical considerations for patent defendants and plaintiffs in responding to infringement bills.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency of defenses
rubrics_metrics.description: Any number of defences may be joined in the same answer provided they are consistent with each other; defences are consistent when they can all be true.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inconsistent defences create a repugnancy which is fatal to the answer unless cured by abandonment of an antagonistic claim. Defences that cannot both be true are inconsistent and will destroy the answer (examples and case citations in text).

rubrics_metrics.name: Particularity of affirmative defences
rubrics_metrics.description: Each defence must be distinctly and affirmatively stated, with such particularity as to time, place, person, and circumstances that the plaintiff may be informed of the precise attack he has to meet.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The answer must apprise the plaintiff of the defendant's theory as to the scope and meaning of the patent so the plaintiff can prepare; hypothetical defenses based on possible future constructions of the patent cannot be set up.

rubrics_metrics.name: Answer must state defendant's theory of patent construction
rubrics_metrics.description: The answer must apprise the plaintiff of the defendant's theory as to the scope and meaning of the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is required so the plaintiff may perceive under what view of the invention the defences will be urged; the defendant cannot rely on hypothetical constructions to be later given by the court.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defendant bound by his answer / limitation on departures
rubrics_metrics.description: The defendant is concluded by his answer, which is regarded as embracing his actual and entire defence, and cannot depart from it except by amendment under leave of the court.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Particularly strict where the plaintiff is entitled to an answer under oath; amendments require leave and may be restricted to avoid prejudice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Affirmative defences must be alleged and proved (prior knowledge)
rubrics_metrics.description: Affirmative defences, especially that of prior knowledge, must be properly alleged as well as proved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assertions of prior knowledge/use must be pleaded with sufficient detail (see many cited cases); mere general allegations of prior knowledge are insufficient to admit evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defences not set up in the answer are waived
rubrics_metrics.description: Defences not set up in the answer will not be considered by the court.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Special defences that in actions at law must be set forth in a notice must in equity appear in the answer, and failure to set them up generally precludes reliance on them later.

rubrics_metrics.name: Special defences in equity: precision and completeness
rubrics_metrics.description: Special defences in equity appear only in the answer and their statement is governed by the same rules as to precision and completeness which are applicable to a notice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When alleging surreptitious procurement, fraud, or similar matters, the answer must set forth distinct, particular, and positive allegations; general language is inadequate.

rubrics_metrics.name: When alleging surreptitious procurement / priority by another
rubrics_metrics.description: If the answer asserts that the patentee surreptitiously or unjustly obtained the patent for what was in fact invented by another, it must also allege that the first inventor was using reasonable diligence in adapting and perfecting it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This requirement hearkens to statutes and case law; mere accusation of surreptitious obtainment without alleging the first inventor's diligence is insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior use / knowledge pleading requirements (names, residences, place)
rubrics_metrics.description: When denying novelty on the ground of prior use or knowledge, the answer must recite the names and residences of the persons using or having knowledge of the invention, and sufficiently describe the place of use to put the plaintiff in possession of the means of identifying such invention with his own.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An allegation of prior use on the defendant's 'knowledge and belief' is insufficient unless the underlying information is disclosed; failure to name users/places generally renders prior-use evidence inadmissible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior use: identify inventors/users, not witnesses
rubrics_metrics.description: A defendant who relies on a defence of prior use must set out in his answer the names of those who invented or used the anticipating device, but not the names of his witnesses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Depositions or testimony from persons not named may only show the state of the art, not establish the prior use for the defence, unless the answer is amended or proper notice given (various cited cases).

rubrics_metrics.name: Depositions/evidence of prior use admissibility depends on pleading
rubrics_metrics.description: Depositions as to prior use cannot be read unless the persons using or who had knowledge were named in the answer; evidence of prior use given by witnesses not named can be considered only to show the state of the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence taken without proper notice may sometimes be struck out; in some circumstances an answer may be amended post hoc and evidence allowed to stand if omission was inadvertent and no surprise resulted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foreign prior use and foreign patents: pleading limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Unless the answer denying priority gives notice of the persons and places of the previous use, evidence of foreign patents and other foreign evidence in support of the answer is not regarded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence of prior use abroad is not supported by notice of use in this country; foreign prior patents not set up in answer can only be used to show state of the art, not as full defence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Denial of priority must cover whole invention
rubrics_metrics.description: The answer denying priority of invention must cover the whole invention, not a part of it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Partial denials that only attack part of the invention are insufficient to open full prior-use evidence (see Parks v. Booth).

rubrics_metrics.name: Machines or items relied upon must be set up in the answer
rubrics_metrics.description: Machines not set up in the answer cannot be offered in evidence nor considered on final hearing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the defendant intends to rely on particular machines/devices, they must be specifically alleged in the answer; omission forfeits their admissibility absent amendment and lack of surprise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abandonment/use-and-sale pleading (two years rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: An answer of use and sale before the application must allege an abandonment, or that the use and sale were more than two years before the application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If abandonment is relied on it must be specially set up; public use and sale and abandonment may be set up in the same answer but not in the same allegation because they depend on different principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defence of non-patentability vs. required plea
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain defenses (for example, that the invention was not patentable) may, in some holdings, need not be set up in the answer; other defences (prior patent or prior publication) must be set up in the answer and not by special plea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There is case law nuance: some invalidity grounds should be pleaded, others may be raised differently; consult controlling authority. Text cites Hendy v. Golden State Miners' Iron Works and Camrick v. McKesson for contrasts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific pleading required for fraud, re-issue discrepancies
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the defence rests upon the fraud of the patentee or upon the departure of a re-issued patent from its original, the answer must charge the fraudulent acts or want of identity in distinct and special allegations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: General statements that 'patent was obtained by false representations' are too vague; distinct language and distinct proof are required (cases: Blake v. Stafford, Doughty v. West).

rubrics_metrics.name: Denial of plaintiff's title: reveal facts affecting record title
rubrics_metrics.description: When the defendant disputes the title of a plaintiff shown by Patent Office records, the answer must reveal the facts which qualify the record title or create antagonistic or exclusive interests in others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the defendant claims equitable assignment/ownership, he must state the consideration paid (nature and amount) so its adequacy may be traversed; failure to do so will not suffice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Traverse of infringement: must be positive and unambiguous
rubrics_metrics.description: The answer must traverse the allegation of infringement positively and without equivocation; a traverse may be couched in general terms referring to the patent as the one covered by the suit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unless the defendant contests the infringement in his answer, very slight proof will sustain the allegation. Denials must be sufficiently specific to allow evidence against them unless counsel stipulates otherwise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Admission effects: admissions are conclusive but limited
rubrics_metrics.description: Admissions in an answer are conclusive on the defendant but have no effect beyond the necessary import of the words (e.g., 'making and selling' implies only the making and selling of one article unless plural used).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Admissions bind the defendant as to what they concede; indirect admissions are as binding as affirmative ones. Parties should plead carefully because admissions limit later contention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Admissions may amount to concessions on novelty/usefulness
rubrics_metrics.description: An allegation in the answer that the defendant has patented the invention since the issue of the plaintiff's patent is a concession that it is both new and useful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such admissions can have collateral legal consequences and should be avoided unless deliberate; see cited cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect and strategic use of sworn answers
rubrics_metrics.description: The plaintiff is entitled to an answer under oath, but since later statutes made parties competent witnesses, it is often wiser not to require a sworn answer; a sworn answer is treated as the testimony of one competent witness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sworn answers constrain the defendant to verifiable facts and may help avoid fruitless inquiry, but they are powerful evidence (often equal to the plaintiff's testimony) and may be difficult for the plaintiff to overcome at trial. Corporations cannot themselves swear; officers must be made parties if a sworn answer is demanded.

rubrics_metrics.name: If admitting use but claiming agency or license, disclose principal / license terms
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the defendant admits use but excuses it by acting as agent or under license, the answer must disclose the principal or show that the license warrants the use made.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An assertion of agency must name the principal; a license defence must show the license's scope covers the acts complained of. Otherwise the admission may be treated as an admission of infringement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Estoppel facts must be specifically pleaded
rubrics_metrics.description: Facts which constitute an estoppel in pais should be set out in the answer with sufficient detail to indicate that if established they will operate as an equitable bar.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Admissions in the pleadings do not prevent setting out the facts which create an estoppel; but the answer must supply the detail from which an estoppel would arise (see Paetz v. Bransford).

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural rule: objection waiver and timing for evidence taken without notice
rubrics_metrics.description: Witnesses produced without proper notice must be objected to at the time or the defect will be waived; evidence taken without due notice may nevertheless be allowed to stand unless a motion to strike it out is made.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where evidence admitted without proper notice is relied upon, appellate courts may reverse if prejudice results; the defendant may sometimes cure omissions by amending the answer if omission was inadvertent and plaintiff not surprised.
